Orestes is a central figure of Greek mythology and tragedy, condemned and redeemed by conflicting moral imperatives. Son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, he becomes a matricide when he avenges his father's murder, an act that triggers divine punishment in the form of the Furies. His story, most fully told in Aeschylus' The Oresteia, becomes a meditation on justice, redemption, and the transition from primitive vengeance to rational law.

After his father Agamemnon is murdered by Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus, young Orestes is spirited away and raised in exile by his sister Electra's intervention. As an adult, Orestes returns and kills both his mother and her lover, fulfilling the mandate of blood vengeance, yet simultaneously committing the ultimate sin of matricide. Duty and law collide. The Furies pursue Orestes relentlessly, driving him to madness as punishment for shedding his mother's blood, even though he acted to avenge his father. The divine law is contradictory.

Aeschylus' Oresteia trilogy traces the moral and legal evolution from tribal blood vendetta to Athenian democratic justice. Orestes' trial becomes the trial of civilization itself. In Sophocles' Electra, his sister becomes a co-conspirator, and their psychological bond complicates the moral calculus of revenge. The siblings' collaboration makes the crime simultaneously justified and damned. Orestes becomes a symbol of the man trapped between irreconcilable duties—filial loyalty and maternal obligation—demonstrating that some moral situations admit no innocent solution.

Euripides' Orestes presents the character as unstable and violent, questioning the heroism of his act. Different tragic poets arrive at different moral conclusions about the same myth. The Oresteia introduces Athena as mediator, transforming blood-vengeance into juridical process. Reason and democracy replace tribal violence, and Orestes becomes the first man acquitted in court. He embodies the civilization whose mythology he inhabits and whose justice system he helps define, while the Furies become the divine enforcers of blood-guilt who pursue him until reason and law intervene.
